summary: This informational RFC publishes the articles of incorporation of the Internet Society for the IETF community, at the request of the poisson working group. It is a legal document rather than a technical specification.

eli5.summary: The official paperwork that says how a big club was set up.

subtitle: The legal articles that established the Internet Society as a non-profit organization

tldr.problem: The Internet Society, which had been informally coordinating Internet development, needed formal legal status as a non-profit corporation to operate effectively.
tldr.mechanism: These articles of incorporation, filed with the District of Columbia, establish ISOC as a non-profit corporation without capital stock. The articles define the board structure, member rights, and the corporation's educational, charitable, and scientific purposes.
tldr.outcome: The Internet Society became a formal legal entity authorized to carry out the evolution of the Internet and conduct educational activities. The articles specify an initial board of fourteen trustees.

today: RFC 2134 is an Informational RFC that documents ISOC's legal establishment. The Internet Society continues as the entity described in these articles and remains the primary organizational home of the IETF and the development of Internet standards.

sections.title: Articles of Incorporation
sections.content: This RFC publishes the formal articles of incorporation of the Internet Society filed with the District of Columbia. The articles establish ISOC as a non-profit corporation without capital stock, operated exclusively for educational, charitable, and scientific purposes. The document was requested by the poisson working group for publication to the IETF community.
sections.eli5: These are the official rules for how the Internet Society works. It is a club set up to help the Internet grow and teach people about it.

sections.title: Purpose and Governance
sections.content: The articles declare that ISOC's purposes include facilitating and supporting the technical evolution of the Internet as a research and education infrastructure, educating the scientific community and public about Internet technology and applications, promoting educational uses of Internet technology, and providing a forum for exploration of new applications. The corporation is governed by a Board of Trustees (not a typical board of directors). The initial board consists of fourteen trustees named in the articles, including figures such as Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn. Net earnings must not benefit trustees or officers privately, and no part of the organization's activities may involve propaganda or political campaigns.
sections.eli5: The club is run by a board of trustees. It helps the Internet grow, teaches people about it, and makes sure it benefits everyone, not just rich people.

sections.title: Structure and Dissolution
sections.content: The articles provide for classes of members whose rights are defined in bylaws. The initial registered office was located at C T Corporation System in Washington, D.C. For amendments, at least four-fifths of trustees must agree, except that unanimous consent is required to amend the fundamental governance article. If the corporation dissolves, all assets must be distributed exclusively to educational, charitable, or scientific organizations qualifying for tax exemption under Section 501(c)(3) of the U.S. Internal Revenue Code.
sections.eli5: The club has members and rules in bylaws. If the club ever ends, all its money goes to other educational groups.
